An anisotropic vacuum breaking (ANGB) involves the spontaneous breakdown of continuous symmetries in systems where Lorentz invariance is already absent, such as solids. This phenomenon was initially analyzed by Son and Oogsten using a specific model of charged superfluids. This work revisits the ANGB through the lens of effective field theory, demonstrating that it can be viewed as the emergence of an additional Nambu-Goldstone (NG) mode beyond the standard two associated with the spontaneous breakdown of Lorenty and internal symmetries. This extra NG mode corresponds to the breaking of the "affine" symmetry group, which is the combined structure of Lorentz transformations and internal symmetry operations. The analysis employs the AFV model of charged superfluids to illustrate this extra NG mode explicitly. The work concludes by examining the stability of this state against the formation of color-magnetic condensate within the context of the AFV model.

Recent research indicates that neural sequence labelers suffer from imbalanced performance, distinguishing significantly higher precision for individual token predictions compared to whole-phrase ones. While previous work attempted to rectify this through weighted loss adjustments or auxiliary components, these methods remain ad-hoc and offer only partial mitigation. We introduce a straightforward yet potent strategy: utilizing large language models (LLMs) to generate weighted, differentiable counterfactual losses for entire phrases. Our approach involves training an LSTM classifier on a dataset of NLP tasks, feeding it LLM prompts with erroneous ground-truth outputs, and having the LLM propose various differentiable counterfactual modifications to those phrases. This shared differentiability allows for backpropagation through both the LLM and its generated text to calculate phrase-specific losses during training. Experiments across five distinct natural language inference (NLI) and text classification benchmarks demonstrate that our method boosts overall accuracy by 2.5% to 5.0% relative to the baseline, yielding a notably sharper improvement in performance for phrase-level prediction.
This paper determines both the chromatic number and the equitable, sum-distinguishing neighborhood total chromatic number for various classes of circulant graphs.

Remote epitaxy is proposed as a strategy to produce Heusler films with a single interface free of van der Waals gaps. Achieved by transferring mechanically exfoliated graphene onto sapphire substrates, this method repels epitaxial growth through the use of graphene as a template, thereby eliminating one of the film's interfaces from direct interaction with the substrate. Employing this approach, we successfully grew Mn2Au on the graphene layer, confirming through photoemission spectroscopy and atomic force microscopy that epitaxial alignment occurs exclusively at the vacuum interface, while perfect crystallinity is maintained across the entire structure. Finally, we demonstrate that adjusting the epitaxial interface count by selecting different van der Waals materials allows for the independent control of interface characteristics and interfacial thicknesses.

A linear code $C$ defined over the ring $\mathbb{Z}_ {p} \mathbb{Z}_{p}^{2}$ has a specified rank $s$ when its generator matrix contains $s$ columns that form a $\mathbb{Z}_ {p} \mathbb{Z}_{p}^{2}$-basis for the associated vector space $\mathbb{Z}_ {p} \mathbb{Z}_{p}^{2}$-module $M$. This work investigates the linear codes over $\mathbb{Z}_ {p} \mathbb{Z}_{p}^{2}$ by initially analyzing the module $M$ derived from this space to determine its $\mathbb{Z}_ {p} \mathbb{Z}_{p}^{2}$-linear generator matrices and corresponding $s$ values. Subsequently, the study focuses on the parameters of dual codes, as well as the construction of codes over $\mathbb{Z}_ {p} \mathbb{Z}_{p}^{2}$ utilizing linear codes from both $\mathbb{Z}_ {p}$ and $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$

This study evaluates various strategies for designing polymer slug injection profiles, focusing on maximizing oil recovery within a specific reservoir and well configuration. The analysis considers multiple design approaches, including constant slugs with fixed attributes, alternating slugs where properties vary periodically, and continuous polymer floods. Performance outcomes indicate that a constant slug design delivers superior results compared to both continuous flooding and an alternating slug design.

In the context of recommendation systems, users typically interact with only a small number of items, yet these items represent a broad diversity. However, existing methods that model user preferences often rely on aggregating actual interactions, which are sparse and limited in scope. This paper proposes a new approach to mining implicit information contained within single-label samples. The core idea involves leveraging the structural relationships among items to infer a user's broader preferences based on their interactions with one specific item. We introduce a new class of "multi-label samples" that encapsulate these inferred preferences. Using this concept, we develop a new algorithm that integrates these samples into standard collaborative filtering workflows. Empirical results indicate that this method significantly improves the performance of popular two-stage baselines across multiple datasets.

This paper examines the heat and Nernst-Planck equations under time-fractional differentiation within a bounded domain, differentiating between fractional orders representing Caputo and Riemann-Liouitz derivatives. By employing analytical techniques, we derive an explicit formula for the upper bound of energy and demonstrate its monotonic decrease over the domain. These expressions are presented as a novel contribution to the existing literature.

We present a categorical description of the Stone-von Neumann theorem, which asserts that any two irreducible representations of an irreducible Heisenbb group on a complex Hilbert space having the same dimension are unitarily equivalent. Our approach involves analyzing representations of categorical algebras and states within the 2-category **Hilb** of Hilbert spaces, linear operators, and *unitary* transformations. Specifically, we demonstrate that a categorical representation of the Weyl (categorical) form of the Heisen group is completely determined by its "pure" states and their transition probabilities.

The origin of high-energy gamma-rays in radio galaxies remains debated, with the two leading theories being jets and accretion-related structures at the disk's center. We propose that significant gamma-ray emission can also arise from magnetically arrested disks (MADs). Utilizing the general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulation framework "general," we generated models of MADs across a broad range of parameters, including black hole mass ($10^8$–$10^{10} M_{\odot}$), spin ($0$–$1$), and specific disk conditions. Our results indicate that gamma-ray luminosity in these systems can reach $10^{44}$–$10^{47}$ erg s$^{-1}$, potentially explaining observed emission in local radio galaxies. This phenomenon is tied to specific, high-energy magnetic reconnection events within the inner disk regions where field strengths exceed $10^4$ Gauss. Such strong fields are characteristic of the MAD state, which emerges when substantial magnetic flux is transported from the disk's outer regions. We find that black hole spin significantly influences the emitted gamma-ray output, with maximally spinning black holes ($a=1$) producing luminosity roughly ten times greater than non-spinning ones ($a=0$). Consequently, gamma-ray observations can serve as a probe for black hole spin. We further demonstrate that gamma-ray signatures in nearby radio galaxies can persist for millions of years,

This study examines the normality assumption of portfolio returns across diverse investment contexts, ranging from passive market exposure and active stock selection to asset allocation and options strategies. We analyze the third and fourth statistical moments of return distributions generated by long-only or long/short positions in individual securities. Our findings indicate that passive market exposure in single-name instruments results in portfolio return distributions with elevated kurtosis and skewness relative to broad market benchmarks, whereas active book strategies can manipulate these moments through tailored positioning. Additionally, we evaluate the impact of options hedges and enhancements on the risk profile of active portfolios. Empirically, our analysis covers the S&P 500, individual tech giants (Apple, Microsoft, Google, Amazon), active tech sector allocations, and specific options-based strategies.

Cardiac auscultation serves as a primary method for diagnosing cardiac diseases, yet current automatic systems struggle with the complex nature of heart sounds, particularly when subjected to environmental interference. This study introduces a robust heart sound classification framework designed to address noisy acoustic backgrounds and the resulting degradation of Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) feature extraction capabilities. The proposed method integrates a two-stage strategy: initially, a Short-Time Fourier Transform (STF) converts heart sound signals into spectrograms, which are then refined using a specialized denoising autoencoder (DAN) to eliminate additive noise. Subsequently, a CNN utilizes these cleaned images to classify the heart sounds. The framework was evaluated using the PhysioNet Computing Challenge 2017 dataset, evaluating three scenarios with varying noise levels. Results indicate that the method achieves a 0.805 F1-score in noise-free conditions, improving to 0.745 and 0.705 scores when noise levels increase to 20 dB and 10 dB, respectively.

The rapid advancement of Internet of Things (IoT) and wearable devices has enabled the collection of vast amounts of personal health data, facilitating significant breakthroughs in diagnosing and treating diseases through data-driven analytics. Nevertheless, concerns regarding data privacy and security have driven the emergence of federated learning (FL), a decentralized paradigm allowing model training across distributed nodes without transmitting raw data. Although FL effectively mitigates privacy risks, it struggles when deploying models across different user populations due to heterogeneity in data distributions and limited sample sizes, necessitating an approach that accounts for these statistical discrepancies. To address this, this paper proposes Federated Transfer Learning for Health (FedHealth), a new framework integrating FL with transfer learning. By leveraging source domain knowledge to enhance target task performance, FedLearning ensures consistent model accuracy despite underlying heterogeneity. Extensive experiments conducted on two major public datasets demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms existing baseline methods.

This study examines various methods of portfolio optimization that incorporate higher moments like kurtosis. This paper categorizes these strategies by the specific higher moments considered and analyzes the statistical distributions assumed for portfolio returns. It further explores the relationship between optimization outcomes and the inclusion of additional moment criteria. Finally, several open questions in this field are identified for future research.

We examine the dark energy density within a string theory compactification framework, analyzing how compactification moduli and Kähler parameters influence its value. By leveraging recent findings on energy densities in string theory brane-bulk configurations, we demonstrate that the cosmologically observed dark energy density can be accounted for in this manner. Specifically, we propose that the required non-zero density arises from the energy concentration near rational points on the compactification manifold's moduli space. Additionally, we identify a rational dependence between dark energy density and the overall volume of the manifold, suggesting that the apparent coincidence in the universe's energy sectors may stem from the inherent discreteness of the rational point structure in string theory.

In today's fast-paced world, individuals often face overwhelming workloads, making it difficult to dedicate sufficient time to every task. To address this challenge, we have developed an innovative solution: an automated application processing system designed to handle and organize incoming requests. This user-friendly tool allows applicants to submit their data via a web form, after which the system automatically generates a professional PDF application. By streamlining administrative tasks, this application ensures that users can dedicate more time to activities they truly enjoy.

This study examines a switching control problem where switching costs are cadlag (having possible jumps), and the cost function depends on the duration between consecutive switches. The objective is to determine an optimal set of switching times that minimizes the total cost, which includes both the cost of switching events and the underlying system dynamics. The paper establishes the existence of this optimal strategy and investigates the characteristics of the cost associated with a single switch. The findings regarding the cadlag nature of the cost function and the continuity of the value function are utilized to derive an dynamic programming approach, specifically the PDE form of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation, for scenarios involving just two switches. The derived HJB equation is demonstrated to possess sufficient conditions for optimality. The study concludes with a concrete illustration drawn from the context of optimal execution in financial trading.

This study investigates asymmetric vector leptoquark pair production at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), challenging previous analyses that assumed symmetry. By integrating the formalism of effective lepton number with specific assumptions about the LHC's electron asymmetry, we present findings on signal characteristics and background noise. Our results indicate that even a modest level of electron asymmetry allows for significantly enhanced signal significance in detecting leptoquarks of spin-2 or higher, even if their production cross-sections remain comparable to symmetric scenarios. Furthermore, the observable impact of asymmetry extends to leptoquarks of spin-1, affecting both statistical significance and the inferred limits on their cross-sections. These conclusions are robust against variations in the degree of asymmetry and the mass of the leptoquark particle.

Temporal measurements of biological systems are frequently characterized by high dimensionality and sparse data, posing significant challenges for statistical modeling and machine learning applications. To address these issues, we introduce a supervised framework utilizing a novel class of hierarchical Bayesian models designed to analyze short, high-dimensional time series. Our approach integrates a sophisticated dimensionality reduction technique that captures complex nonlinear dependencies among variables. This method employs a sparse, time-varying, latent nonlinear index which is continuously updated across the observation period. We demonstrate the efficacy of our model through simulations and by analyzing a specific dataset comprising gene expression levels from a pancreatic islet sample.

We examine the far-infrared and submillimeter spectral lines of neutral carbon (C{\sc i}) in two distinct molecular gas reservoirs: nearby galaxies and the circumgalactic medium (CGM). Our findings indicate that these C{\sc i} transitions generally do not follow the standard radiative transfer models of local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) or the standard two-level system. Instead, the excitation of the three fine-structure lines in nearby galaxies appears driven by subthermal mechanisms, specifically collisions between atoms and photons. In the galaxy CGM, the excitation likely results from a combination of subthermal processes and photoexcitation by the ultraviolet background.

This subthermal excitation is a critical factor when utilizing C{\sc i} observations to characterize the physical conditions of molecular clouds. Furthermore, the optical depth of the 1.57 mm line ($\lambda$1.57 mm) serves as a sensitive probe of the reservoir's total neutral carbon content. Consequently, the C{\sc i} lines offer a viable method for detecting and measuring molecular gas on large scales, extending well beyond the limits of traditional tracers like CO.

We propose a model featuring vector-like composite quarks that simultaneously addresses recent anomalies observed in both neutral meson mixing and the decay rates of $B$ mesons. This model introduces two new vector-like quark generations, designated as $(U', D')$ and $(\tilde{U}, \tilde{D})$, with mass scales around a few TeV. These quarks generate significant contributions to $B_s \to \mu\mu$ and $B_s \to J/\psi \mu\mu$ processes via both direct terms and mixing effects, while simultaneously explaining the $B_{d,s}$ mixing phenomena through box diagrams involving new charged scalars. Furthermore, the model remains consistent with existing LHC constraints.

In the sequence reconstruction problem, an array of finite length containing items from a limited set is accessible only through intersecting subsequences of a fixed length, where access to any specific subsequence occurs with a probability less than one. The objective involves determining whether the complete original array can be deduced from these partial observations, with the constraint that access patterns for any given line are independent and random. This study examines permutations arranged in a $1$-dimensional Bose-Dacus framework, utilizing a specific distribution of reads and evaluating success probability through the lens of the Hamming distance.

This study introduces a hierarchical few-shot classification framework designed to enhance performance in the HMR task within the context of automatic musical instrument detection. The approach treats the problem as a classification challenge involving groups of instruments, where each group functions as a hierarchical structure. By organizing instruments into a hierarchy, the system enables the model to generalize across instruments that share similar characteristics. Empirical evaluation on a newly created classification benchmark, developed from the original MIDI-instrument dataset, demonstrates that this hierarchical framework surpasses a flat classification baseline.

We introduce a dataset comprising 2,300 questions paired with answers derived specifically from research articles. Our goal is to evaluate whether large language models (LLMs) can generate accurate, grounded responses to inquiries that require searching within their encyclopedic knowledge, using academic papers as a defined constraint. Analysis reveals that current top-tier LLMs achieve an F1 score of 0.31 for question-answering tasks on this dataset, indicating significant room for improvement. Furthermore, researchers utilizing our data observed a 2.5% enhancement in question-answering accuracy and a 1.5% boost in question-generation performance on three standard benchmarks after fine-tuning their models on the new dataset.

Pulsar Timing Arrays are emerging as a novel method for detecting gravitational waves from supermassive black hole binaries in eccentric inspiraling configurations. We present a simulation of such signals that incorporates full post-Newtonian (PN) accuracy in the waveform, utilizing a fast algorithm requiring minimal memory. When paired with an efficient folding technique, the simulation generates an orbit's worth of full-time series for a binary with a shrunk-down timescale factor of $10^{-6}$ in just 0.01 seconds on a dual-core processor. Our analysis demonstrates that while the traditional quadrupole approximation suffices for most PTA applications, adopting higher-order waveform expressions is essential for precisely matching the spectral distortions caused by eccentricity. Furthermore, we note that the spectral splittings generated by eccentricity are significantly more pronounced than the amplitude modulations typically associated with these signals.

This work offers a retrospective on mathematical modeling of epidemic outbreaks, utilizing the current pandemic of SARS-CoV-2 as a case study. Our examination focuses on the historical development of the SIR model, specifically tracing how refinements to its parameters enabled the estimation of key epidemiological indicators, such as the basic reproduction number ($R_0$) and effective reproduction number ($R_t$), as well as the assessment of non-pharmaceutical intervention efficacy. We further investigated the historical application of optimal control theory within these models to analyze containment strategies. Finally, we explored the integration of these frameworks with statistical inference methods to calibrate model parameters and generate reliable forecasts.

Acronyms are a common feature in English that offer space-saving benefits, yet they create comprehension barriers when readers lack knowledge of their expanded forms or when the meaning is ambiguous. Although numerous research efforts have attempted to automate acronym creation and clarify their meanings, no singular solution currently exists. To address this gap, we introduce **Shiitake**, a Web-based platform designed for the automatic identification and resolution of acronyms. Key capabilities of this system include the management of term glossaries for specific domains, the generation of acronym-related information from domain-specific resources, and the provision of curated suggestions for expanded forms.

We propose a scheme for atom-molecule conversion involving three Lithium atoms, where the kinetic energy of a second atom enables the formation of an ultracold dimer through laser illumination. This approach circumvents the standard requirement for an initial ultracold trimer state by addressing a two-body threshold instead of a more stringent three-body one. We detail the underlying principles, including the creation of a bound state from two atoms bound to a third scattering partner, and present calculations of the conversion rate. Our results indicate that molecules produced in this manner possess slightly higher energies relative to dissociation limits compared to those generated from ultracold trimers. Nevertheless, subsequent evaporative collisions between these molecules and atoms could facilitate further cooling to the ultracold dimimer regime.

We introduce DNAStore, a file system designed to optimize DNA data storage by integrating hierarchical directory structures and updating individual files. Our approach addresses two primary challenges inherent to DNA: the difficulty of modifying data after synthesis and the low throughput of the writing process. To overcome these, we translate file updates into new storage sequences, leveraging the high efficiency and rapid throughput of DNA synthesis for generating entire new files or entire directories. We conducted experiments using both in vitro DNA storage and a realistic cloud simulation. Our findings indicate that DNAStore achieves a 99.5% data retrieval accuracy, reduces reconstruction latency by 99.9%, and cuts storage costs by 99.5% compared to naive methods.

Topological insulators and semi-metals have become a focal point of research in condensed matter physics, optics, and photonic sciences over the last few decades. A significant breakthrough in this field has been the discovery that certain topological properties can be defined by the properties of nodal lines in momentum space, including Dirac, Weyl, and Majorana lines, as well as higher-dimensional topological features. This review examines the theoretical frameworks and recent experimental and numerical realizations used to define topological invariants associated with these structures. Special attention is given to platforms such as metamaterials, photonic crystals, optical systems, and circuit quantum electrodynamics, highlighting their shared capacity to realize these phenomena.

Brain tumors represent a prevalent and perilous neurological disorder, demanding rigorous diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment planning. Medical image analysis utilizing deep learning has become a vital tool in this domain, offering significant advantages in speed and precision. In this study, we propose Multi-task Attention Guided Net (MAG-Net), a novel deep learning architecture designed to segment and classify brain tumors via MRI images. This framework employs parallel convolutional branches to extract hierarchical features from MRI data, which are subsequently refined through feature selection modules to mitigate redundancy. A feature fusion module then integrates these enhanced features to generate the final output. Extensive experiments conducted on the publicly available BraTS 2019 dataset demonstrate that MAG-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance, yielding Dice Similarity Coefficients of 0.921 for segmentation and an accuracy of 0.985 for classification.

Increasingly, differentiable rendering engines are being utilized to support optimization tasks in computer vision and graphics, including light estimation, material decomposition, and inverse problems in image formation. A critical challenge in differentiable synthesis for these applications is the efficient computation of soft shadows, which are essential for providing accurate image-based gradients. This paper introduces a new differentiable model for soft shadow calculation that remains computationally efficient. The associated optimization landscape for these soft components is smooth, free of discontinuities, and lacks sharp local minima. Evaluations demonstrate that this approach achieves a speedup of 1.7 to 2.5 times compared to state-of-the-art methods while delivering higher quality results for material and light estimation.

Interlace is still a common method for capturing and storing video, yet each interlaced frame consists of two separate fields with alternating horizontal lines. Converting these to full, solid pictures improves quality for both viewing and further analysis. Even though progressive output is required, the original interlaced data carries motion that standard conversion removes, causing visible artifacts like jagged lines or shimmering. To eliminate these issues, deep learning models have recently been developed, but they run too slowly to process video in real time. This paper introduces a new network called the Real-time Interlace conversion Network (RinNet), which can run at speeds exceeding 100 frames per second on a single GPU. Tests show that RinNet runs more than three times faster while delivering superior results compared to existing methods.

An analysis is conducted of the root mean square radius characterizing the neutron distribution across various nuclear systems, comparing non-relativistic and relativistic mean-field approaches. The study focuses on how this radius responds to changes in the neutron skin and the overall charge radius of the nucleus.

Adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) is essential for accurately resolving the shock discontinuities frequently found in high-Mach number flows. However, the inherent adaptivity of AMR grids complicates the application of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which typically require fixed structures. To overcome this, we propose a deep learning approach that utilizes a fixed grid to directly predict refined solutions on a coarse mesh. This method is tested on one- and two-dimensional shock tube problems, as well as in two-dimensional scenarios involving reflection shocks and contact discontinuities. Results indicate that this method achieves a significant reduction in computational cost while maintaining high accuracy, effectively predicting solution features such as shocks and rarefaction waves with precision.

High-dynamic-range (HDR) imaging is achieved by merging multiple exposures with varying levels of exposure, a technique essential for capturing scenes with extreme contrasts between light and dark areas. Although cameras swapping exposures automatically previously lacked the ability to record such high dynamic ranges due to restricted exposure intervals, this paper presents an HDR method feasible on smartphones that utilizes the natural variability of unstructured image collections. The proposed approach first identifies the optimal exposure for every picture in the set and subsequently merges the selected exposures to create the final HDR image. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that this strategy successfully achieves a 10.5-log dynamic range when leveraging the inherent scene diversity found in casual photography.

Causal deep learning represents a significant advancement over conventional supervised methods, offering improved generalization and the capacity to build interpretable models. Nevertheless, integrating causal deep learning into real-world scenarios remains challenging. To address this gap, we introduce a comprehensive survey that clarifies the fundamental concepts, architectures, training strategies, and evaluation methods of causal deep learning. We specifically examine the intricacies of aligning correlations with true causality within complex neural networks and provide a thorough review of various data- and model-driven approaches designed to induce causal representations. Finally, we outline numerous emerging research avenues, offering a foundational roadmap for future causal deep learning endeavors.

This study employs rapid magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to noninvasively capture temperature profiles within a gas-solid fixed bed. As the specific heat capacity of the solid particles is too low for conventional thermocouple methods to measure effectively, this study utilized electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) contrast agents to facilitate temperature mapping via MRI. In a fluidized bed, heat exchange occurs when hot gas enters and interacts with cooler solids. The experiment involved introducing 4 mm glass beads preheated to 523 K into a reactor at 298 K, while monitoring temperature distributions at 0.5-second intervals over a 10-second duration. The resulting MRI data revealed that the solid particles reached thermal equilibrium with the ambient environment within 10 seconds.

This note demonstrates that the long-standing Mumford conjecture follows directly from the short-term validations of both the n!-conjecture and Penner's map as established in recent work. Specifically, we prove that the source term $b$ satisfies the conditions necessary to invoke the source term $b$-principle.

This study presents a performance evaluation of various multilevel preconditioners used within a cardiac mechanics simulation. The research evaluates the Geometric Multigrid (GMG), Algebraic Multigrid (AMG), Schur complement multigrid (SMG), and a hybrid method combining GMG and SMG. All techniques were implemented in a cardiac simulation framework based on a fully discrete, monolithic discretization using the Discontinuous Galerkin (DG) method on a 3D cardiac mesh. This setup facilitated simulations on a high-performance computing system with up to 16,000 cores, enabling performance analysis across a range of mesh resolutions and preconditioner configurations. The results demonstrate that the hybrid SMG/GMG method offers a robust solution, requiring fewer levels and fewer applications to cardiac simulations. The authors conclude that this hybrid approach is an optimal choice for cardiac simulations, delivering strong performance within a simulation framework.

The author has derived universal formulas for computing mixed moments of traces within certain random Hermitian matrices featuring independent entries. These findings allow for determining all $O(n^{-2})$ corrections to the first moment and the $(n^{-1})$-level individual eigenvalue correlation functions. Previous work by the author established similar universal formulas restricted to cases where partitions are non-crossing; however, the new formulas apply generally to arbitrary partitions. The derivation relies on novel combinatorial techniques and connects these formulas to the theory of orthogonal polynomials. A significant portion of the combinatorial component is presented in an appendix, which also includes a joint work result with A. Sodin regarding the asymptotic behavior of specific monic orthogonal polynomial systems.

Promotional videos serve as a vital marketing asset for businesses, yet their creation remains labor-intensive and costly. Although traditional automation methods exist, they often yield rigid and uninspired outputs. Consequently, there is a growing interest in leveraging artificial intelligence to enhance both the automation and persuasiveness of these videos. This interest is driven by the convergence of robust large language models (LLMs) and advanced multimodal generation tools. However, the field currently lacks a comprehensive review of AI-assisted persuasive video generation. To address this gap, this paper surveys the subject by introducing an overarching framework for AI-enabled persuasive video generation, which encompasses three core components: understanding the marketing context, adapting content to specific audiences, and synthesizing the final video. We further examine emerging trends, including the integration of LLMs and video generation capabilities, as well as opportunities for future research.

Security professionals often face the challenge of detecting users' complacency, a phenomenon where a diminished perception of risk leads to negligent security practices. This study introduces a novel methodology for quantifying the True Sense of Security (SSS), defined as an individual's accurate recognition of risk levels. The proposed approach integrates a quantitative assessment of the False Sense of Security (FSS)—calculated as the discrepancy between a person's self-assessed security and the actual security status—with a qualitative evaluation encompassing the underlying causes of FSS. To illustrate this framework, the authors analyze data from a large-scale smartphone security survey involving 1,000 participants, offering a structured method to better understand user behavior regarding cybersecurity.

Acoustic metagratings are periodic surface structures designed to manipulate sound waves through diffraction, enabling applications in beam steering, sonic imaging, and noise control. While traditional acoustic metagratings made of macroscopic mechanical components suffer from limitations such as inertia, limited frequency ranges, and manufacturing constraints, this study introduces microacoustic metagratings at the microscopic scale. These innovative structures were fabricated using two-photon lithography, achieving a period of 100 micrometers capable of operating at frequencies up to 1.6 kHz. Experimental results demonstrate successful generation of sound diffraction at ultra-high frequencies, with the ability to manipulate acoustic beams and create acoustic shadows. Furthermore, the design principles for these microacoustic metagratings offer a pathway to overcome the inherent limitations of conventional macroscopic mechanical diffraction systems.

Standard diffusion, exemplified by the Brownian motion solution to the Fokker-Planck equation, is characterized by Gaussian distributions whose evolution follows a simple scaling of variance. This study explores deviations from such normality and fixed scaling by introducing random diffusivity into the diffusion framework. Specifically, we analyze the problem where initial conditions remain deterministic but evolve under initial random fields of diffusivity, focusing on two models: the constant-flux (DF) and linear (LF) random diffusivity. These random parameters cause particle ensembles to depart from Gaussian behavior, resulting in distributions defined by more complex integral expressions. We demonstrate that these complex initial random fields induce either superdiffusion or subdiffusion, depending on the specific random diffusivity model applied, and notably generate heavy-tailed distributions. Furthermore, we derive a general formula for the time-dependent entropy of an arbitrary initial distribution within these random diffusivity contexts.

We present a rigorous theory that addresses linear and Kerr nonlinear coupling between arbitrary modes within dielectric optical resonators. By deriving a generalized nonlinear overlap integral, we determine the frequencies, spatial field distributions, and evolution of these coupled modes. Our approach applies broadly to various optical devices, encompassing waveguides, microring resonators, photonic crystal cavities, and nonlinear directional couplers. Additionally, we develop an analytical framework specifically addressing Kerr interactions in circularly symmetric systems, such as those found in ring resonators and waveguides. This model accounts for the interaction of any two modes—regardless of whether they are degenerate or distinct—and is validated against numerical simulations. The predictive framework established here offers a foundational tool for the design of contemporary and future optical technologies.

This work investigates systems governed by ordinary differential equations where controls are functions of time and may be unbounded. Under assumptions of Lipschitz continuity and the existence of a control Lyapunov function within specific classes, sufficient conditions are established for the origin to be globally exponentially stabilizable. These requirements are satisfied, for instance, by periodic systems exhibiting average dissipativity or by non-autonomous systems possessing uniform asymptotic stability with Krasovskii functions. Furthermore, the paper derives direct links between these functional classes and the well-known Bohl–Bernstein property, which ensures that every bounded solution persists indefinitely. Finally, the results are applied to time-varying linear systems to demonstrate the practical use of the proposed theoretical framework.

This study introduces a deep learning framework utilizing generative adversarial networks (GANs) to recover high-resolution turbulent velocity fields from low-resolution data across various Reynolds numbers. The theoretical basis for this approach lies in the fact that turbulent structures at small scales exhibit Reynolds-number-independent behavior, allowing the model to reconstruct flows at different Reynolds numbers using training data from a single reference case. Results indicate that the proposed method achieves superior accuracy compared to standard bicubic interpolation and a large-eddy simulation (LES) framework operating at the same resolution. Furthermore, the model demonstrates the ability to accurately reproduce Reynolds stress tensors at interpolated Reynolds numbers that were not included in the training dataset.

It is a common misconception in standard quantum theory that the concept of a wave function evolving according to the wave equation is incompatible with the formalism itself. In this work, we challenge that view by utilizing the momentum representation within the theory of a free particle to construct a scenario where the wave equation is explicitly upheld.

Current research into confidence calibration has primarily focused on closed-world settings, often neglecting the significant epistemic uncertainty that arises when models encounter out-of-distribution inputs. Consequently, networks tend to generate overconfident predictions for such unfamiliar data. Addressing this issue, we introduce a novel framework for open-world uncertainty modeling that utilizes an auxiliary energy model to refine primary network predictions. By integrating these components into the main architecture, the system avoids the need for additional inference-time computation. Extensive experiments conducted on ImageNet and a real-world deployment at the CLEVR dataset demonstrate that this energy-based approach substantially outperforms existing open-world state-of-the-art methods.

Process discovery and monitoring are essential for the lifecycle of business processes. While existing approaches often rely on complex, resource-intensive data structures, this paper introduces a method for converting business process models into declarative monitoring and discovery rules using stream processing. By leveraging event streams as the input format, the proposed technique offers a more efficient and effective solution for both discovering and monitoring processes. Additionally, the authors present a novel process discovery algorithm based on this method, demonstrating its efficacy through a case study on the extended X-ray process.

Light propagation in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals (PQCs) is characterized by a typical transition where eigenstates shift from extended to confined states, creating an eigenstate gap mirroring that found in random systems. This study introduces an additional transition within the eigenstate gap of 1D PQCs: reentrant delocalization. We demonstrate its existence theoretically via a tight-binding model and verify it experimentally using laser beams. Furthermore, we attribute this phenomenon to the interference between two distinct mechanisms of light scattering.

The application of quantum entangled photons in spatial mode multiplexing allows for the simultaneous transmission of multiple data streams over a single mode, offering a robust solution against decoherence. This study investigates super-resolution imaging by reconstructing the real-time intensity distribution of individual modes during demultiplexing. Results indicate that reconstructing the superposition state of two S0 modes yields a resolution of 0.71 times the diffraction limit, whereas doing so for two L0 modes achieves a resolution of 0.57 times the diffraction limit.

This expository note explores the connection between algebraic and analytic approaches to compactifying moduli spaces. It begins by outlining the necessary background in algebraic geometry and then transitions to the specific context of moduli spaces, focusing on the degeneration of compact complex surfaces with ample canonical classes. The article concludes by demonstrating how these analytic methods can be interpreted through an algebraic framework.

This study examines the resilience of a two-timescale Lotka-Volterra ecosystem, specifically focusing on identifying early warning indicators of abrupt shifts in population dynamics. We analyze how bifurcations and critical slowing-down phenomena serve as such indicators, analyzing their dependencies on system parameters. Additionally, we propose a change-point detection algorithm designed to recognize these shifts in real-time. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a low false positive rate, with performance improving as the duration of system observation extends.

The galaxy luminosity function exhibits a pronounced upturn at the bright end, a feature that parallels the observed relation between stellar mass and star formation rate (M*-SFR), which peaks around $10^{11} M_{\odot}$ before declining at higher masses. While the physical mechanisms driving this turnover at high stellar mass remain unclear, we investigate the potential influence of bulges by analyzing the $M*-SFR$ relation separately for bulge-dominated and bulge-deficient galaxies. Our findings indicate that the turnover occurs exclusively in the high-bulge fraction, whereas star formation continues to rise with total mass in galaxies lacking significant bulges. Furthermore, we observe a negative correlation between bulge fraction and SFR, suggesting that the turnover is caused by the suppression of star formation in massive bulges rather than in the rest of the galaxy. Consequently, our results suggest that the growth of the galaxy mass function at high masses and the subsequent turnover in the $M*-SFR$ relation are intrinsically linked to the formation of bulges.

Cache Coherence is a critical challenge in multicore architecture, and self-invalidating memory addresses serve as a key mechanism for enabling efficient private caching in meshes and wormhole networks. While self-invalidating addresses are typically defined by their domain boundaries, existing approaches rely on static definitions that fail to adapt to dynamic changes in a network's topology. To address this limitation, we propose a static initialization method for self-invalidating domains that dynamically evolves throughout the network's lifecycle. Our approach utilizes a set of logical rules to define domain boundaries, introducing two primary techniques: self-downgrading and self-invalidation. The self-downgrading process allows domain boundaries to expand gradually, whereas self-invalidation immediately collapses boundaries upon detecting a breach. We evaluated our method against static domain definitions across a range of benchmarks, observing that static domains derived from our self-defined domain rules deliver a 1.5% to 10.5% performance improvement over traditional static approaches.

We strengthen the conclusion of Freiman's $3k-4$ theorem (which applies when $3n < |A+B| \leq 4n$ for a $k$-element set $A$) by proving that if the inequality holds as $3n \leq |A+B| \leq 3k-4$, then $A$ is necessarily a subset of an arithmetic progression of length $3n - |A+B| + 2$. In particular, our result tightens the threshold previously established by the authors themselves, who demonstrated that for $|A+B| \leq 3k-4$, $A$ fits within an arithmetic progression of length $3n - |A+B| + 1$.

The primary objective is to identify conditions under which this trajectory possesses Hausdorff dimension exceeding $1/H$ while simultaneously ensuring the image set holds positive Lebesgue measure and contains a non-empty open region.

To address these inquiries, the paper leverages connections between the occupation time density and the distribution of the maximum value. A pivotal contribution involves characterizing the event where the process attains its global maximum over $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, specifically analyzing the probability that the supremum over the path coincides with the process value at some time $t$. Utilizing these insights, the article establishes criteria for the image set to exhibit full measure properties. Using Dirac's variational method with the Jackiw-Kerman function, we examine the dynamics of the H\'enon-Heiles model. Our analysis highlights a clear correspondence between the model's regular and chaotic trajectories and their associated Lyapunov exponents. We identify specific chaotic orbits and calculate the positive Lyapunov exponents for two such instances. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the chaos indicators of the model and its associated Lyapunov exponents.

X-ray imaging serves as a primary diagnostic tool for detecting COVID-19, yet identifying patients who require ICU admission based on these images remains challenging. This study introduces a new dataset comprising CT scans of COVID-19 patients, categorized into two groups: those who were subsequently admitted to the ICU and those who were not. We developed a baseline model utilizing a fully connected neural network to classify ICU admission potential based on these x-rays. Additionally, we investigated the link between the number of visible pulmonary lesions in the scans and the likelihood of ICU admission. Our findings indicate that CT scans from patients admitted to the ICU exhibit a higher count of pulmonary lesions compared to those discharged to other settings or home.

The classical universal bundle functor $W: s\mathrm{Grp}(\mathcal{C}) \to s\mathrm{Set}(\mathcal{C})$, defined on simplicial groups within a category $\mathcal{C}$ equipped with finite products, can be extended to operate as a monad on s\mathrm{Grp}(\mathcal{C})^. This extension enables the formulation of a similar universal Monad, $U$, applicable to s\mathrm{Grp}(\mathcal{C})^. Consequently, this result permits the construction of a universal Monad for s\mathrm{Grp}(\mathcal{E})^, the category of sheaves of groups on a manifold $M$.

This paper examines the causes behind false positives in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD), a critical yet under-investigated aspect of the field. We analyze the dataset annotations and propose a new metric called Dataset Annotation Complexity (DAC), which measures how difficult it is to distinguish between supported and incorrect relationships based solely on training data. Our analysis reveals that the official COCO dataset annotations suffer from high complexity, leading models to frequently mistake them for hallucinations. Furthermore, we identify two primary causes for these errors: (1) the presence of similar but unlabelled instances in the data, and (2) inherent ambiguities within the labels themselves. To address these issues, we introduce a new training objective known as Relationship Contrastive Loss (RCL), designed to differentiate positive from negative relationship samples. Experiments show that incorporating RCL yields a significant boost in precision for relationship detection, resulting in more accurate visual reasoning.

We introduce Delta Sampling Raster Action Recognition (delta Sampling R), a method designed to enhance action recognition under challenging conditions involving low light and data scarcity. This sampling strategy captures video frames with varying intervals, creating a diverse and dense representation of events that improves recognition accuracy. Experiments indicate that delta sampling boosts performance by 1.3% and 2.1% over linear sampling on the MSRAction360 and MSRLocaton360 datasets, respectively, with improvements in the 200+ class subsets reaching 1.3% and 3.0%. Additionally, this sampling approach enables effective learning from as few as 100 labeled videos for each action category.

This study examines a galaxy group at redshift $z \approx 3$ using deep Hubble Space Telescope imaging. The most prominent member is a massive system characterized by a stellar mass of $\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot}) = 11.1$, a stellar disk exhibiting significant stellar mass asymmetry (lopsidedness), and a central bulge comprising $\approx 10\%$ of the total galaxy mass. Detailed spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling reveals that the bulge consists primarily of stars older than 1 Gyr, with negligible recent star formation ($\log(\text{SFR}) < -3$ $M_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$), identifying it as a quiescent structure. The outer disk shows clear signatures of ongoing star formation, with the asymmetric arm located on the side of enhanced activity. The convergence of the outer star-forming arm and the inner quiescent core suggests a scenario where the bulge originated from the accretion of a satellite galaxy. This process likely triggered the development of the lopsidedness and simultaneously induced a star formation burst in the outer regions, while the resulting dynamical effects suppressed further stellar activity in the central area.

The authors propose a novel statistical framework designed to rigorously evaluate the significance of the universal texture zero within the neutrino sector, addressing this issue through rigorous statistical evaluation.

We investigate the nonlinear critical elliptic equation
$-\Delta u + u = |u|^{1.4}u + |u|^{4}u$ in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.
Our analysis reveals the existence of a continuous family of solutions exhibiting periodic blow-up.
Furthermore, we establish that the total number of such blow-up solutions is one.
As a secondary outcome, our work provides a positive answer to a conjecture by Frank and Soavero regarding the scenario of a single blow-up solution.

Current state-of-the-art neural architectures for source code prediction struggle with two key issues: their inability to incorporate domain-specific knowledge and a propensity to generate syntactically invalid code. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel modular system for the neural generation of high-level programs. This approach employs a generative probabilistic procedural language (PPLe) as a mediator, enabling the composition of learned atomic program fragments. Furthermore, we enhance this framework with a static analysis module designed to refine predictions and eliminate semantic errors. Experiments conducted on a dataset of Python list processing functions demonstrate that this method significantly outperforms current leading models, yielding a 20% improvement in execution success rates and a 10% boost in code completeness metrics.

On November 7, 2004, the Neutron Spectrometer aboard the Advanced Composition Explorer (ACE) detected a significant increase in low-energy protons (within the 0.5–2 MeV range). This event followed a solar flare and an associated coronal mass ejection (CME) that occurred at 15:18 UTC on the same date. Analysis indicates that these energetic protons resulted from the decay of solar neutrons, which had been trapped within magnetic fields in the solar corona. The onset of the proton signal detected by ACE coincided with the arrival of a shock wave and the associated solar energetic particle (SEP) event at the location of the satellite.

We examine the dispersion relations of linearized perturbations within a specific formulation of viscous hydrodynamics. This approach adheres to both second and first principles regarding thermodynamics, incorporates linear response theory, and maintains a direct connection to ideal hydrodynamics through an invariant mapping. By expressing transport coefficients using standard notations, we derive and analyze their corresponding linearized dispersion relations. Furthermore, we investigate the stability conditions imposed by various dissipation frameworks. Our findings indicate that while these linearized relations align with those predicted by linear response theory, the hydrodynamics remain unstable when coefficients are defined via the formalism of second-order response.

Streaming anomaly detection is a critical task in data mining, yet existing methods often overlook the necessity of incremental analysis and fail to account for the evolving nature of concept drift in data streams. To address these gaps, we introduce a new approach known as InQMAD for anomaly detection within continuous environments that also adapt to drift. The method leverages quantum machine learning to compute the Mahalanobis distance between new incoming samples and the historical profile, facilitating anomaly identification. Specifically, InQMAD utilizes the Histogram quantum machine learning technique to estimate this distance efficiently. The proposed algorithm has been rigorously assessed using both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating superior performance against leading baseline methods.

This paper examines the legal standing of government-ordered decryption under the Fourth, Fifth, and Sixth Amendments. It proposes a verification-based analytical framework to evaluate such compulsion and applies this model to various decryption scenarios, including full, partial, and password-derived unlocking. Additionally, the article offers an overview of modern cryptographic concepts and their practical relevance to these legal debates.

Regarding the legal concepts discussed:
- **The First Amendment**: Not the focus of the analysis.
- **The Fourth Amendment**: Protects against unreasonable searches and seizures.
- **The Fifth Amendment**: Protects against self-incrimination.
- **The Sixth Amendment**: Guarantees the right to counsel.

**Decryption Types:**
1. **Full Decryption**: Uncovering the entire contents of a storage medium.
2. **Partial Decryption**: Revealing only specific files or data points.
3. **Password Derivation**: Forcing the creation of a password through compelled testimony.

**Verification Approach:**
This method involves checking the consistency of the government's claim with observable facts, similar to verifying a search warrant's scope.

**Cryptography:**
Modern encryption algorithms and key management are explained to demonstrate their importance in understanding the limits of decryption orders.

**Right to Counsel:**
The availability of legal representation is considered a factor in the overall analysis.

**Self-Incrimination:**
The analysis explores how decryption compulsion intersects with the privilege against forced confession.

We propose a general model for simulating measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution. This framework is built upon a basic protocol, allowing researchers to easily adapt it to various variants by modifying the related parameters. Additionally, the model's flexibility supports the incorporation of specific characteristics inherent to real-world systems, such as the error rates of physical components, the presence of pulse-pair attacks, and side-channel leakage. As a practical application, we utilize this model to analyze the Twin-Beam type of MDI-QKD, demonstrating how it can be used to evaluate the impact of asymmetric pulse energies on system performance.

This work presents a general-purpose polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs), applicable to any class of problem instances admitting a Fréchet-Hausdorff PTAS. This broadens previous findings, which were limited to binary CSPs or those with uniform weights. The novel technique leverages a novel, general method for constructing nearly optimal CSP solutions from any given set of points.

This study introduces a novel numerical scheme designed to approximate solutions for specific Fokker-Planck equations, with applications to both stochastic control and mean field games. The proposed method integrates a time-stepping technique, a spatial Lagrange element of high order, and a symplectic scheme known as the Lagrange-Galerian method (as per the source, which describes a scheme combining a symplectic technique with high-order spatial Lagrange elements). The authors establish the existence of a discrete solution, demonstrate its uniqueness under a Courant condition, prove convergence toward the solution of an implicit high-order scheme, and provide an estimate of the convergence rate.

The rapid advancement of deep learning has driven significant breakthroughs in artificial intelligence, particularly within image recognition, speech analysis, and natural language processing. Despite these achievements, Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) often function as "black boxes," making their internal decision-making processes difficult to comprehend. This paper offers a comprehensive review of current methods used to interpret and visualize the relationships, patterns, and structures inherent in deep learning models. We examine various visualization techniques, including those applied to the network's architecture, input representations, intermediate computational layers, and final output mechanisms. Furthermore, this research reviews explanation methodologies categorized by the point within the system—covering global and local interpretability—and by the specific component targeted, such as the weights, neurons, or activation functions of the network. Finally, we outline several open challenges in the field of visualization and interpretability of deep neural networks, concluding with observations on future investigative directions.

Observations indicate that a significant number of Red Giant Branch stars possess rapid rotation and high chromospheric activity, which is unexpected since these stars should undergo significant spin-down. We utilize 3D stellar evolution models to examine the conditions required for surface rotation to increase, specifically focusing on scenarios where stars consume their planets. Our simulations reveal that if a star consumes a Jupiter-mass planet, the surface rotation can rise by a factor of two, while activity levels can surge by an order of magnitude. However, this phenomenon is not universal; it depends critically on the efficiency of angular momentum transport, particularly the operation of the specific core-overshoot mechanism. Our results suggest that surface spin-ups occur only when the specific core-oversight efficiency parameter ($\alpha_{\rm CO}$) is at least 0.01. Conversely, if stars are spun up by other mechanisms, the observed population of rotating red giants implies a minimum cumulative mass of planets consumed of approximately $0.01\,M_{\odot}$.

Rapidly spreading online, fake news poses a significant threat to public well-being, prompting the development of various detection systems. A primary hurdle for these systems is the scarcity of labeled data, which hinders model training and generalization. While Neural Process (NP) frameworks offer a viable solution by learning from limited labeled inputs and generalizing to unlimited unlabeled data, they struggle with complex, structured information found in multimedia content like images and text. Furthermore, fake news often relies on inconsistencies between modalities that current detectors fail to capture. Addressing these issues, we introduce Meta Meta NP (M³NP), a meta model designed to detect fake news across diverse domains using minimal training data. This system integrates a text and image processing module to handle high-level semantic features and employs a cross-modal attention mechanism to learn inter-relationships that reveal fabrication. Evaluations on two major benchmarks demonstrate that M³NP significantly surpasses state-of-the-art methods in its ability to generalize to unseen data.

This study examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation defined by $\partial_t u + \partial_x u = F(u)$, with initial condition $u(0,x) = u_0(x)$, where $F$ is a smooth function of one variable and $\partial_x$ denotes the spatial derivative on the torus $\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$. When $F$ corresponds to a smooth, strictly increasing function with a Lipschitz constant less than 1, we identify necessary and sufficient conditions on the initial data $u_0$ required for the solution to develop a singularity at a specific time $T>0$ and location $x_0\in\mathbb{T}$. We further derive an explicit formula for the blow-up rate and the singular value at $(t,x_0)$ as $t$ approaches $T$ from below. These findings extend prior work by the authors regarding the Burgers equation ($F(u)=u^2$) found in the references [10, 11] and the work of J. M. Fraas and J. L. Vázquez [12, 13] on the porous medium equation ($F(u)=\sqrt{u}$).

The primary objective is to derive the steady-state joint age-demand distribution and evaluate the long-term average age. A closed-form expression for the steady-state age is provided, contingent upon specific assumptions regarding the demand generation process. The study further analyzes the system performance across various discrete-time demand generation processes. The primary contribution of this work lies in the derivation of a steady-state distribution for the discrete-time demand generation process, which is essential for assessing the performance of the proposed AoF framework. The study finds that the long-term average age is significantly influenced by the characteristics of the demand generation process, particularly its variance and mean inter-arrival times. We present a family of quasi-compact monoidal algebras, including a specific sub-class of quasi-bialgebras, derived from regular, invertible, and non-degenerate set-theoretic solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation. The deformation parameters involved are defined by the eigenspaces resulting from the eigenvectors of the permutation and braiding operators associated with these set-theoretic solutions. The construction method relies on the utilization of a specific quasi-antitriple structure inherent to the set-theoretic solutions. Additionally, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for these set-theoretic solutions to yield the output quasi-bialgebras.

Recent research has focused extensively on Golay complementary arrays (GCA), which have emerged as a preferred alternative to Golay complementary sequences (GCS) for radar and communications applications aiming to mitigate interference. This study introduces two novel methods for generating real-valued GCA that utilize the concept of generalized Golay complementary quadruplets (GCQ). The first method constructs GCQs by combining pairs of GCS based on specific correlation properties, utilizing a deterministic formula to form the resulting GCA directly. The second method employs GCQs created through convolution of GCS and achieves higher densities of GCQs by leveraging a recently developed coding algorithm for GCQs. Simulation outcomes indicate that both approaches produce GCQs and GCAs with the desired correlation characteristics, while the first method guarantees a GCA density of 50%.

Quantum interference within silicon's atomic lattice offers a pathway to control quantum states, yet experimental validation remains limited. This study presents scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) evidence of quantum valley interference between two degenerate valley states in silicon, revealing a spatial modulation of current with a lattice periodicity. Furthermore, we demonstrate atomically precise spin exchange interactions mediated by varying bias-induced electrostatic potentials. These findings establish silicon as a viable platform for constructing complex quantum circuits.

Complex systems, characterized by their numerous interacting components, frequently exhibit behaviors that are difficult to predict due to their inherent intricacy. A prominent example is the evolution of social networks, where new nodes and edges emerge continuously, and the interplay between existing elements drives the development of novel structures. Addressing such challenges requires a capacity to discern patterns within these intrinsically dynamic and evolving architectures. This study introduces a unified framework for modeling the temporal progression of network topology through Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). By leveraging this approach, we demonstrate the model's efficacy in forecasting node additions, edge formations, and the overall topology of both social and technological networks.

We introduce an infinite family of recursive equations designed to enumerate binary integer partitions meeting specific constraints on their consecutive parts. This work extends a prior result by the author that identified the number of partitions satisfying only a single part constraint. In addition to providing explicit characterizations of the two allowed part types, this article demonstrates several connections to combinatorial objects in algebraic and stable homotopy theory, including partitions of Euclidean space, the enumeration of spaces within the mod $p$ Moore fibration, and the $A_\infty$-space structures associated with Moore $G$-spaces. Finally, this paper also offers a combinatorial interpretation of odd-indexed Fibonacci and Lucas numbers, as well as their even indices, as counts of these constrained binary partitions.

Lerner segmentation is a critical step in the planning of radiation therapy therapy, yet it remains challenging due to the scarcity of annotated data. To mitigate this issue, we propose a deep learning framework that generates synthetic brain lesions to augment datasets. Our approach employs a three-stage architecture: a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) extracts image features, which are then utilized by two interconnected modules—a Progressive Adversarial Variational Auto-Encoder (PAVE) that generates synthetic lesion masks and a combination framework for integrating these synthetic masks with healthy brain imagery. Evaluations on the BraTS 2015 and 2019 challenges demonstrate that augmenting data with our proposed framework enhances performance in terms of Dice scores and Kappa coefficients.

Strong quantum nonlocality is demonstrated for unextendible product bases (UPB) within certain heterogeneous multipartite systems. This finding indicates that the inherent nonlocality of UPBs can be amplified by embedding a quantum system into a larger multipartite framework composed of heterogeneous subsystems. Specifically, a bipartite UPB is transformed into a multipartite state exhibiting strong quantum nonlocality through this method. The results further reveal a connection between the classical correlations present in pure product states and quantum orthogonality graphs, suggesting a pathway to construct the minimal number of particles required for such nonlocality.

The fifth data release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS-V) aims to map one-quarter of the milky way's stellar population, a goal supported by the highly capable APOGEE-2 instrument. This system relies on two SDSS astrobots, which are designed to autonomously control telescopes and spectrographs while executing complex, interdependent tasks. Coordinating these robots requires a comprehensive coordination protocol that accounts for all individual and joint actions, constraints, and objectives. This paper introduces a practical method for generating such complete coordination frameworks, which is subsequently validated using a concrete scenario where astrobots schedule a series of APOGEE observations.

GP 2 is a programming language designed to be compiled into C, leveraging a compiler that employs a context-sensitive type inference system. This system relies heavily on a complex, interdependent network of type dictionaries. This text describes the upgrade to the GP 2 type checker implemented in the new context. The revised algorithm is straightforward, easy to code, and guarantees termination. It also leverages the homomorphism between the grammar of type constraints and that of dictionaries. This text text describes how the implementation is carried out in practice and presents performance results.

Feature extraction through deep learning has become a cornerstone in numerous data analysis tasks, yet the availability of extensive, well-annotated datasets is not always guaranteed. To mitigate this dependency, the proposed method introduces a unified framework designed to integrate diverse pre-trained models and apply them within a consistent architecture. This framework supports various forms of labeled and unlabeled data, offering adaptable strategies for feature embedding, classification, and overall system optimization. Empirical evaluations across seven distinct data classification tasks demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art performance, particularly when utilizing labeled datasets.

Model selection for categorical variables is essential in both categorical and ordered regression frameworks, requiring methods capable of addressing the inherent high dimensionality. This study introduces a novel approach for model selection in regression settings that integrates a specific penalty designed to eliminate categorical predictors. We establish theoretical bounds for the proposed method, demonstrating its superior performance compared to existing alternatives. Empirical evaluations, utilizing simulations as well as real-world datasets, confirm these findings.

Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable general capabilities, enhancing their ability to perform complex reasoning using specialized knowledge remains a significant challenge. We introduce SKILL (Structured Knowledge Infusion for LLMs), a novel framework designed to improve reasoning via structured information from knowledge graphs. Central to this approach is the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) paradigm, which supplies relevant graph data for specific tasks. However, current RAG methods often underutilize graph structures, leading to suboptimal performance. To address this, we developed a new embedding technique that converts graph nodes into structured representations, enabling LLMs to reason more effectively over graph-organized information. We evaluated SKILL on two datasets: FreeBQA, drawn from the Freebase knowledge graph, and WikiQA, sourced from Wikipedia. The results indicate that SKILL outperforms both standard RAG methods and fine-tuned LLMs on these benchmarks.

This review examines recent developments in nonlocal diffusion models, with a focus on frameworks that yield coherent limits—both practical and theoretical—converging to classic local diffusion operators and fractional Laplacians. We explore various definitions of nonlocal differential operators and operators characterized by nonlocal domains, analyzing their convergence to target local and nonlocal counterparts. Additionally, we address existence and uniqueness results for operators with consistent limiting behaviors, highlighting applications in diverse fields such as image processing, population dynamics, and material science.

We introduce a new constrained optimization framework for generating minimal surface solutions in stitched panoramic views that respect the priority of gravitational orientation. Gazing at a flat screen from standing or seated positions, the human visual system naturally perceives a view consistent with upright gravity; consequently, image content is warped via a diffeomorphic transformation to align its implied horizontal plane with the actual gravitational horizon. This phenomenon, known as "vignetting," allows viewers to overlook discrepancies in the foreground and background relative to the composition's internal horizon. While our earlier work presented a method for creating such effect-free single images through local geometric warping, this paper extends that technique to create viewing zones free of distortion across an entire area of interest. This is achieved by integrating a closed minimal sheet surface with an opening shaped like a polyhedral polyhedron constructed from multiple camera intrinsics and extrinsics. By formulating this as a global constrained optimization problem, we derive a computationally efficient algorithm that yields a seamless, distortion-free visual experience for standing users across a broad spatial range.

Miatle's proof regarding the vanishing of Eisenstein series for $GL(m,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$ when the Kassen parameter $\delta$ satisfies $1<\mid s\mid$ heavily relies on detailed properties of the Weyl group orbit summation for Dirichlet series coefficients, specifically their multiplicative structure. This article examines several combinatorial aspects underpinning these properties, with a particular focus on the instances where $m=4$ and $m=5$.

We introduce a biophysical computational model of basal ganglia circuits, parameterized using data from non-human primate imaging and electrophysiology, that successfully replicates the effects of dopamine depletion observed in these animals.
